title: Energy harvesting from a rotating gear using an impact type piezoelectric MEMS scavenger

sections.heading: ENERGY HARVESTING FROM A ROTATING GEAR USING AN IMPACT TYPE PIEZOELECTRIC MEMS SCAVENGER
sections.text: P. Janphuang, D. Isarakorn, D. Briand, and N.F. de Rooij Ecole Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), Institute of Microengineering (IMT), Sensors, Actuators and Microsystems Laboratory (SAMLAB), Neuchâtel, Switzerland

sections.heading: ABSTRACT
sections.text: This paper reports on energy harvesting from an impact by using a piezoelectric MEMS scavenger. Useful electrical power is generated by the impact of the rotating gear on the MEMS piezoelectric transducer. The design of the device structure was based on both analytical and FEM models for the estimation of induced voltage generated from piezoelectric transducer. A prototyping of piezoelectric MEMS based impact harvester consisting of a piezoelectric unimorph transducer was operated on a gearbox with a speed of $2 5 ~ \mathrm { r p m }$ . For the cantilever type harvester occupying approximately $4 . 2 ~ \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ , an average output power of $1 . 2 6 \mu \mathrm { W }$ was measured across a resistive load of $2 . 7 \mathrm { M } \Omega$ .

sections.heading: KEYWORDS
sections.text: Impact energy harvesting, piezoelectric, MEMS, rotating gear, PZT

sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
Vibration energy harvesting has attracted an amount of interest as a means for powering low-power electronic devices and various types of sensors. It not only provides regenerative energy source, but also offers an advantage for systems in which battery replacement is challenging. The development of energy harvesters to scavenge energy from vibration has rapidly advanced during the past few years because motions and vibrations are the most ubiquitous ambient energy source available, like in industrial machines, transportations, and human body. There are three types of transduction methods including electromagnetic, electrostatic and piezoelectric for ambient vibration energy harvesters. Among these methods, piezoelectric materials have received much attention due to the conversion of vibration energy into electrical energy with a high power density and high conversion efficiency, potential miniaturization with simple structure, and mass manufacturability [1].

Several piezoelectric MEMS harvesters have been proposed and investigated over the years and most of them are based on resonant mass spring systems. To optimize the power generation, the harvesters have to be excited very close to its resonant frequency, typically more than $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ [1-5]. Harvesting energy from the lower frequency, such as in motions of human body or moving objects, which are typically less than $3 0 ~ \mathrm { H z } ,$ , is also attractive and comes with great challenges. Using a mass spring system requires a high mass to resonate at lower frequencies, resulting in low power density and being harder to scale down with MEMS technology. For this reason, an alternative principle of piezoelectric harvesters in which a mechanical impact is applied by direct contact on a piezoelectric transducer is a promising solution. As for the well known piezoelectric shoe [6] and piezoelectric windmill [7], significant electrical output power can be obtained with this type of harvesters. However, those devices were not based on MEMS technology and only a few studies have been reported on the use of MEMS devices to harvest energy from mechanical impact [2].

In this paper, we present the characteristics and performances of a MEMS harvester based on the impact of a rotating object on a piezoelectric bending structure. The impact type piezoelectric harvester consisting of a $1 3 5 ~ { \mu \mathrm { m } }$ -thick PZT sheet bonded on a silicon AFM like cantilever beam was successfully fabricated. The electrical characteristics of the harvester, i.e. voltage, power and load were experimentally investigated and the results obtained are in good agreement with the analytical model and FEM simulations.

sections.heading: HARVESTING CONCEPT AND MODELING
sections.text:
The concept of the proposed system in this work is illustrated in Fig. 1. It consists basically of a gear driven by an inertial mass system and a piezoelectric transducer located over the gear in order to keep the system as compact as possible. The piezoelectric transducer, which is a cantilever structure in our case, is coupled to the inertial mass system through a tip at the free end of the cantilever. When the gear start moving, the piezoelectric cantilever is set into motion by the impact between the gear teeth and the tip of cantilever. In consequence a part of kinetic energy accumulated in inertial mass system is converted to electrical energy through the impact on piezoelectric structure. Here, the system is demonstrated by using a motor as the inertial mass. A silicon substrate served as a support layer for the piezoelectric material since silicon micromachining allows the easy fabrication of an AFM like cantilever including a silicon tip.

![](images/373a843a0d02d99039c3c3a201bb730a0ab750a72086436030c5a2741af2e9d8.jpg)  
Figure 1: Schematic diagram of the concept for harvesting energy from a rotating object.

Among common MEMS support structures, such as cantilever, bridge and diaphragm, cantilever was chosen since it is the most compliance structure for a given input force and it can generate larger strain compare to bridge and diaphragm structure. For this study, a unimorph piezoelectric cantilever beam structure was constructed.

An analytical model used for the determination of generated electric power from piezoelectric unimorph was accommodated by using the bending beam theory of piezoelectric bimorph reported in [10].

$$
V _ { O C } = \frac { 3 } { 8 } \biggl ( \frac { H } { L } \biggr ) ^ { 2 } h _ { 3 1 } \delta _ { z }
$$

where H: the total thickness of the beam, L: the length of the beam, $\delta _ { z }$ : the displacement of the beam, $\mathrm { h } _ { 3 1 }$ : the piezoelectric constant expressed as:

$$
h _ { 3 1 } = g _ { 3 1 } ( c _ { 1 1 } ^ { D } + c _ { 1 2 } ^ { D } ) + g _ { 3 3 } c _ { 1 3 } ^ { D }
$$

where $\mathbf { g } _ { 3 1 }$ and ${ \bf g } _ { 3 3 }$ : piezoelectric voltage constant, $c _ { 1 1 } ^ { D }$ $c _ { 1 2 } ^ { D }$ and $c _ { 1 3 } ^ { D } :$ piezoelectric elastic stiffness coefficients.

Since the configuration of the harvesting device considered in this work is a unimorph cantilever, its open circuit voltage of the unimorph cantilever can be expressed by:

$$
V _ { O C ( u n i m o r p h ) } = \frac { 1 } { 2 } V _ { O C ( b i m o r p h ) }
$$

The parameters for the unimorph used in the prototype was ${ \bf h } 3 1 = - 4 . 6 2 \times 1 0 ^ { 8 } { \bf V } / { \bf m }$ . The magnitude of h31 was calculated using the materials constant available for the piezoelectric ceramic PZT-5A4E from Piezo Systems, Inc.

sections.heading: DESIGN AND FABRICATION
sections.text:
The design of the impact type piezoelectric harvester was supported by FEM simulation in ANSYS 12.0 to determine the induced voltage generated on the deflection of piezoelectric unimorph. The harvester consisted of a PZT film stacked on a silicon beam. The geometry of the harvester is defined by three main parameters: the area of the beam, the thickness of the support layer and the thickness of the piezoelectric film. As a starting point, a rectangular shape with a length of $5 \mathrm { { m m } }$ and a width of 3 mm was chosen to maximize the size of the capacitor since the potential power output is directly related to this parameter [1]. The piezoelectric layer made of 135 $\mu \mathrm { m }$ -thick PZT-5A was first selected because bulk piezoelectric ceramics can provide greater electromechanical force, structural strength and charge capacity than deposited thin films [3]. The piezoelectric film completely covered the silicon support layer. As demonstrated in [4], to maximize the electrical energy generated from the harvester the ratio of the thickness of the bender $\left( \mathrm { t _ { p } / \ t _ { c } } \right)$ has to be close to 0.64. Due to the thickness of the PZT film the silicon support layer thickness has been defined to be thinner at $1 5 0 ~ { \mu \mathrm { m } }$ to maintain a certain flexibility of the harvester.

In simulation, the tip at free end of cantilever was neglected for simplification and therefore the force or displacement was directly loaded to the free end of cantilever in the direction of approach $z$ -direction). The boundary conditions included displacement constraints in the clamped position of the cantilever to prevent the beam from moving away. Therefore the free end of cantilever was allowed to move only in $\mathbf { Z }$ -direction. The bottom surface of the PZT layer was set as ground and top surface as floating. The variations in tip’s depth, from $2 0 ~ { \mu \mathrm { m } }$ to $1 0 0 ~ { \mu \mathrm { m } }$ , were simulated by applying a corresponding force, from $\phantom { - } 0 . 0 4 \mathrm { N }$ to $0 . 4 \mathrm { N }$ , in the static analysis. Figure 3 shows the generated voltage distributed along the PZT loaded with 0.1N (for $8 \mu \mathrm { m }$ of deflection). The maximum voltage is localized on the nodes at the clamped position of the beam. The average voltage generated through the PZT film thickness can be also simulated by coupling the entire nodes at top surface together in ANSYS [8].

![](images/d16c72a923442f60d1a7ecb2e4b7fa955e7b4c02703d8f0cda8e102ddd8b7359.jpg)  
Figure 2. Schematic of a unimorph cantilever energy harvester with the design parameters indicated.

![](images/4efce2043a50904edd2aa7b6338068828c7008073c125c362e87b4c29501cbcb.jpg)  
Figure 3. Result of FEM simulation for the induced voltage generated by the PZT film.

The fabrication process of the impact type PZT harvester is illustrated in Fig. 4. The process starts from a $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { { m m } }$ in diameter and $3 9 0 ~ { \mu \mathrm { m } }$ -thick silicon substrate. The shape of rectangular cantilevers is first patterned from the top side by DRIE (Fig. 4(a)). A $1 5 0 ~ \mathrm { { n m } }$ -thick LPCVD silicon nitride film is then deposited on both sides for electrical isolation and used as mask during the KOH etching of silicon (Fig. 4(b)). Backside openings in the nitride are defined using UV lithography followed by RIE etching (Fig. 4(c)). The exposed silicon area is wet etched in a KOH solution to accomplish the silicon AFM like cantilever resulting in a silicon tip with a height of $2 4 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ . The bonding of $1 3 5 { \mu \mathrm { m } }$ -thick PZT covered with nickel top and bottom electrodes is performed using spin coated UV curable epoxy (Fig. 4(d)). Fig. 5 shows one of the fabricated impact type PZT harvesters and SEM image obtained from the silicon tip.

![](images/811a3ac39537ba6d5a4fcf09a6f2ca0b1caf07554e453f3fc464b4a1bebf4f18.jpg)  
Figure 4. Fabrication of impact type harvester: (a) DRIE (b) deposition of Silicon nitride (c) RIE on backside (d) KOH etching on back side and (e) bonding of PZT with metallic electrodes by using spin coated UV curable epoxy.

![](images/06fff1220d90e8f757b6ff453f476894ea1825529308ef982f1390e2233a8ad3.jpg)  
Figure 5. Optical images of a PZT/Silicon cantilever and SEM image obtained from the silicon tip (height of 240 µm).

sections.heading: EXPERIMENTS
sections.text:
The energy harvesting performance of the impact type PZT harvester was first investigated by a complete set of experiments on power generation as illustrated in Fig. 6. A gearbox with speed of $2 5 \mathrm { r p m }$ consisting of mini DC motor and a gear with 16 teeth was used as a rotating object and therefore giving the impact to the harvester. The harvester was then mounted on micrometric X,Y and Z stage to precisely adjust the position of the tip over and into the gearbox and connected to an oscilloscope to detect the output voltage from the impact type PZT harvester. A laser Doppler vibrometer (LDV), Polytec OFV 502 fiber interferometer driven by Polytec OFV 3000 vibrometer controller, is used to monitor the displacement of the harvesting device.

![](images/2cab4fc10a330313d64de86951366a6706000cb176e54071b0a73ff7b1445a68.jpg)  
Figure 6. Schematic diagram of the experimental setup used for testing the impact type PZT MEMS harvester.

sections.heading: RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
sections.text:
In the first experiment, the orientation of cantilever over the gear was adapted from the proposed concept, as shown in Fig. 7. This was implemented to avoid the breaking of the cantilever due to the torsional movement induced by the impact of the gear on the silicon tip. This is already a first indication showing that the design of the couple tip-gear, their shapes and the materials used, will have to be considered in the future for a long term reliable operation. ![](images/00a25d2166cd0576e320fde4c87df8b1c4aea54269622af7b95f13f0785c05f0.jpg) Figure 7. Optical image of the harvester mounted on $X ,$ Y and Z stage over the gear box. The power generation from the impact type PZT harvester is observed by varying the depth of the tip into the gearbox. The measured results on the output voltage generated from the impact type PZT harvester and the displacements of the beam obtained as function of the tip’s depth are given in table 1. The results of the analytical model and FEM simulation were then compared to the measured electrical response of the impact type PZT harvester (Fig. 8). A good agreement between measurements, analytical and FEM simulation is achieved. Table 1. Results of the open circuit voltages generated from the impact type PZT harvester for different tip’s depth.

The voltage level depends on the design parameters and electrical load used in the circuit. Figure 9 gives an example of the output voltage peaks measured across load resistors of $1 1 8 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ and $2 . 7 \mathrm { M } \Omega$ . To determine the output power, the harvester was connected with various resistive loads and the generated current through the resistive loads for different tip’s depth was recorded by a multimeter (Agilent 34411A). An average output power of $1 . 2 6 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ was obtained at $1 0 0 ~ { \mu \mathrm { m } }$ tip’s depth with an optimal resistive load of $2 . 7 ~ \mathrm { M } \Omega$ at a gearbox speed of $2 5 ~ \mathrm { r p m }$ (Fig. 10). sections.heading: CONCLUSIONS
sections.text: A novel concept of MEMS based impact energy harvesting from a rotating object using piezoelectric harvester was presented in this work. A piezoelectric MEMS made of a thick PZT sheet bonded on a silicon AFM like cantilever was developed to harvest energy from the rotating gear. The generated voltage of the impact type PZT harvester was analytically and experimentally evaluated and an average output power of $1 . 2 6 \mu \mathrm { W }$ was obtained for a device placed on the gearbox at a speed of $2 5 ~ \mathrm { r p m }$ . As result, the output voltage and power reached a level of interest for practical applications and could be easily increased by using multiple cantilevers on the same gearbox or increase rotation speed. The design of the system architecture, MEMS harvester structure and experiments are on going for the optimization of the output power, the compactness and the reliability of the device.
